headings.title: Introduction to Fetal Circulation
headings.content: Fetal circulation operates differently from postnatal circulation because the lungs do not perform gas exchange in utero. The placenta acts as the organ of respiration, nutrition, and waste elimination for the developing fetus. Oxygenated blood returns from the placenta via the umbilical vein, bypassing the non-functioning fetal liver and lungs through specialized vascular structures. Understanding this baseline is necessary to comprehend how the cardiovascular system reorganizes within minutes of birth.

headings.title: Key Fetal Shunts and Structures
headings.content:
To direct oxygen-rich blood preferentially to the brain and coronary circulation, the fetal heart and great vessels contain three vital shunts:
- **Ductus venosus**: Connects the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, allowing much of the oxygenated blood to bypass the liver.
- **Foramen ovale**: An opening in the interatrial septum that shunts blood directly from the right atrium to the left atrium.
- **Ductus arteriosus**: A vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta, diverting blood away from the fluid-filled lungs.

headings.title: The Trigger: First Breath and Cord Clamping
headings.content: Birth initiates a dramatic cardiopulmonary transition triggered by two immediate events: aeration of the lungs and clamping of the umbilical cord. The first breath expands the alveoli, drawing air into the lungs and clearing fluid. Simultaneously, clamping the umbilical cord removes the low-resistance placental vascular bed, instantly doubling systemic vascular resistance. These two mechanical shifts reverse pressure gradients across the fetal shunts, setting permanent circulatory independence in motion.

headings.title: Pulmonary Vascular Resistance and Blood Flow Changes
headings.content: Before birth, pulmonary vascular resistance is exceptionally high because the small lung blood vessels are constricted in a low-oxygen, fluid-filled environment. When the newborn breathes oxygen and the lungs expand, local vasodilators like nitric oxide are released, causing pulmonary vascular resistance to plummet. Consequently, cardiac output from the right ventricle flows readily into the pulmonary arteries and lungs rather than diverting through the ductus arteriosus.

headings.title: Functional and Anatomical Closure of Fetal Shunts
headings.content:
The temporary shunts close in stages, shifting from functional cessation of flow to permanent anatomical sealing.
- **Foramen ovale**: Closes functionally within minutes of birth due to increased left atrial pressure pressing the septum primum against the septum secundum.
- **Ductus arteriosus**: Constricts within hours due to high blood oxygen tension and a drop in circulating prostaglandins.
- **Ductus venosus**: Closes functionally when the umbilical cord is clamped and eventually fibroses into the ligamentum venosum.

headings.title: Establishment of the Neonatal Circulation
headings.content: Once all shunts close and the pulmonary circulation is fully integrated, the newborn achieves parallel circulation. The right side of the heart now pumps deoxygenated blood exclusively to the lungs, while the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation. This separation ensures optimal tissue oxygenation required for extrauterine life. Nurses monitor vital signs closely during this transitional window to ensure stable hemodynamics are maintained.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Delayed Transition
headings.content: Failure to complete normal circulatory transition leads to serious neonatal complications. If pulmonary vascular resistance remains high, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) occurs, causing continued right-to-left shunting across the foramen ovale or ductus arteriosus. This results in severe hypoxemia and cyanosis. Additionally, prematurity can keep the ductus arteriosus open, leading to left-to-right shunting and heart strain.
